CALIFORNIA GENETIC INFORMATION PRIVACY ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · Jordan T. Reyes

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's Genetic Information Privacy Act, Civil Code section 56.18 et seq. (Chapter 2.6 of the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act) — a state consumer-privacy statute governing direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies' collection, use, and disclosure of consumers' genetic data. It states facts about who the statute regulates, the express-consent categories it requires, the security and consumer-rights mechanisms it imposes, and its enforcement structure, as those may relate to Acme, Inc. This document is distinct from the federal Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA), an employment-discrimination statute covered elsewhere in this collection: the statute described here regulates a company's data practices toward consumers, not an employer's treatment of employees or applicants. This information sheet does not itself constitute a privacy notice, does not obtain any consumer's consent, and does not tell Acme, Inc. whether it is a "direct-to-consumer genetic testing company" under this statute or what to do about any specific product, practice, or consumer request.

WHO THE STATUTE REGULATES: "DIRECT-TO-CONSUMER GENETIC TESTING COMPANY" AND "EXPRESS CONSENT"
The Genetic Information Privacy Act applies to a defined category of entity. Civil Code § 56.18(b)(5) defines a "direct-to-consumer genetic testing company" as an entity that does any of three things: sells, markets, interprets, or otherwise offers consumer-initiated genetic testing products or services directly to consumers; analyzes genetic data obtained from a consumer, except to the extent the analysis is performed by a person licensed in the healing arts for diagnosis or treatment of a medical condition; or collects, uses, maintains, or discloses genetic data collected or derived from a direct-to-consumer genetic testing product or service, or directly provided by a consumer. The statute also defines the consent it requires in a specific way: under § 56.18(b)(6), "express consent" means a consumer's affirmative authorization given in response to a clear, meaningful, and prominent notice about a specific collection, use, maintenance, or disclosure of genetic data. The statute states that express consent cannot be inferred from inaction, and that agreement obtained through use of a "dark pattern" does not constitute consent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Direct-to-consumer genetic testing company” means an entity that does any of the following: (A) Sells, markets, interprets, or otherwise offers consumer-initiated genetic testing products or services directly to consumers. (B) Analyzes genetic data obtained from a consumer, except to the extent that the analysis is performed by a person licensed in the healing arts for diagnosis or treatment of a medical condition. (C) Collects, uses, maintains, or discloses genetic data collected or derived from a direct-to-consumer genetic testing product or service, or is directly provided by a consumer."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.18(b)(5) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Genetic Information Privacy Act, definitions — "direct-to-consumer genetic testing company" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.18.)
  "“Express consent” means a consumer’s affirmative authorization to grant permission in response to a clear, meaningful, and prominent notice regarding the collection, use, maintenance, or disclosure of genetic data for a specific purpose. The nature of the data collection, use, maintenance, or disclosure shall be conveyed in clear and prominent terms in such a manner that an ordinary consumer would notice and understand it. Express consent cannot be inferred from inaction. Agreement obtained through use of dark patterns does not constitute consent."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.18(b)(6) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Genetic Information Privacy Act, definitions — "express consent" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.18.)
  Known gap: Both quotes are subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 56.18 — they are not independent of one another. This clause states the statute's own definitional scope; it does not determine whether any particular entity meets this definition. The statute's own text limits the analysis prong of the definition to entities other than a person licensed in the healing arts acting for diagnosis or treatment, and this clause does not address the statute's separate definitions of "genetic data," "biological sample," "consumer," or "service provider" (also in § 56.18(b) but not quoted here), nor the statute's scope exemptions for certain HIPAA- and Confidentiality of Medical Information Act-covered entities, research institutions, and other categories, which appear in a different section not covered in this document.

REQUIRED PRIVACY PRACTICES SUMMARY AND PRIVACY NOTICE
Before it may rely on the consents described below, the statute requires a direct-to-consumer genetic testing company to make specific disclosures available to a consumer. Civil Code § 56.181(a)(1) requires the company to provide clear and complete information about its data policies and procedures by making available to the consumer a summary of its privacy practices, written in plain language, and a prominent and easily accessible privacy notice containing, at a minimum, complete information about the company's data collection, consent, use, access, disclosure, maintenance, transfer, security, and retention and deletion practices, along with information that clearly describes how to file a complaint alleging a violation of the statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Provide clear and complete information regarding the company’s policies and procedures for the collection, use, maintenance, and disclosure, as applicable, of genetic data by making available to a consumer all of the following: (A) A summary of its privacy practices, written in plain language, that includes information about the company’s collection, use, maintenance, and disclosure, as applicable, of genetic data. (B) A prominent and easily accessible privacy notice that includes, at a minimum, complete information about the company’s data collection, consent, use, access, disclosure, maintenance, transfer, security, and retention and deletion practices, and information that clearly describes how to file a complaint alleging a violation of this chapter, pursuant to subdivision (c) of Section 56.182."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.181(a)(1) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Genetic Information Privacy Act, privacy practices summary and privacy notice requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.181.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subsection, § 56.181(a)(1); no additional independent source was located for it. This clause states the notice-content requirement; it does not address the separate, additional consent requirement of § 56.181(a)(2), covered in a companion clause in this document, does not restate the statute's separate required notice concerning sharing of deidentified data for research purposes, and does not specify the format, length, or delivery method a notice must use beyond what the statute's own text requires.

EXPRESS CONSENT IS A MENU OF SEPARATE CONSENTS, NOT ONE BLANKET CONSENT
The statute does not treat a single consent as covering every use of a consumer's genetic data. Civil Code § 56.181(a)(2) requires a direct-to-consumer genetic testing company to obtain a consumer's express consent for the collection, use, and disclosure of the consumer's genetic data, and states that this includes, at a minimum, separate and express consent for each of several distinct categories: the use of the genetic data collected through the genetic testing product or service itself, including who has access to it, how it may be shared, and the specific purposes for which it will be collected, used, and disclosed; the storage of a consumer's biological sample after the initial testing requested by the consumer has been fulfilled; any use of genetic data or the biological sample beyond the primary purpose of the genetic testing or service and its inherent contextual uses; any transfer or disclosure of the consumer's genetic data or biological sample to a third party other than a service provider, including the name of that third party; and the marketing or facilitation of marketing to a consumer based on the consumer's genetic data, or by a third party based on the consumer having ordered, purchased, received, or used a genetic testing product or service.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Obtain a consumer’s express consent for collection, use, and disclosure of the consumer’s genetic data, including, at a minimum, separate and express consent for each of the following: (A) The use of the genetic data collected through the genetic testing product or service offered to the consumer, including who has access to genetic data, and how genetic data may be shared, and the specific purposes for which it will be collected, used, and disclosed. (B) The storage of a consumer’s biological sample after the initial testing requested by the consumer has been fulfilled. (C) Each use of genetic data or the biological sample beyond the primary purpose of the genetic testing or service and inherent contextual uses. (D) Each transfer or disclosure of the consumer’s genetic data or biological sample to a third party other than to a service provider, including the name of the third party to which the consumer’s genetic data or biological sample will be transferred or disclosed. (E) (i) The marketing or facilitation of marketing to a consumer based on the consumer’s genetic data or the marketing or facilitation of marketing by a third party based upon the consumer having ordered, purchased, received, or used a genetic testing product or service."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.181(a)(2) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Genetic Information Privacy Act, menu of separate express consents (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.181.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subsection, § 56.181(a)(2); no additional independent source was located for it. The statute's marketing-consent category carries its own further conditions and a narrow same-company advertising exception, at § 56.181(a)(2)(E)(ii)-(iii), that are not restated in full here. This clause states which categories require separate consent under the statute's own text; it does not state what form a compliant consent must take beyond the statute's separate "express consent" definition covered in a companion clause, and does not address the revocation mechanism the statute requires once consent is given, also covered in a companion clause.

REVOCATION, SAMPLE DESTRUCTION, DATA SECURITY, AND CONSUMER ACCESS/DELETION RIGHTS
Once a company has obtained the consents described above, the statute imposes several follow-on obligations. Civil Code § 56.181(b) requires the company to provide effective mechanisms, without unnecessary steps, for a consumer to revoke consent after giving it, with at least one such mechanism using the company's primary medium of communication with consumers. Under § 56.181(c), the company must honor a revocation as soon as practicable and no later than 30 days after the consumer revokes consent, and must destroy the consumer's biological sample within 30 days of receiving a revocation of consent to store the sample. Separately, § 56.181(d) requires the company to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices to protect a consumer's genetic data against unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure, and to develop procedures and practices enabling a consumer to easily access the consumer's genetic data, delete the consumer's account and genetic data (except data the company must retain to comply with applicable legal and regulatory requirements), and have the consumer's biological sample destroyed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A company that is subject to the requirements described in paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) shall provide effective mechanisms, without any unnecessary steps, for a consumer to revoke their consent after it is given, at least one of which utilizes the primary medium through which the company communicates with consumers."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.181(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Genetic Information Privacy Act, mechanism to revoke consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.181.)
  "If a consumer revokes the consent that they provided pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (a), the company shall honor the consumer’s consent revocation as soon as practicable, but not later than 30 days after the individual revokes consent, in accordance with both of the following: (1) Revocation of consent under this section shall comply with Part 46 of Title 45 of the Code of Federal Regulations. (2) The company shall destroy a consumer’s biological sample within 30 days of receipt of revocation of consent to store the sample."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.181(c) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Genetic Information Privacy Act, revocation deadline and sample destruction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.181.)
  "The direct-to-consumer genetic testing company shall do both of the following: (1) Implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices to protect a consumer’s genetic data against unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure. (2) Develop procedures and practices to enable a consumer to easily do any of the following: (A) Access the consumer’s genetic data. (B) Delete the consumer’s account and genetic data, except for genetic data that is required to be retained by the company to comply with applicable legal and regulatory requirements. (C) Have the consumer’s biological sample destroyed."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.181(d) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Genetic Information Privacy Act, data security duty and consumer access/deletion rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.181.)
  Known gap: All three citations are subsections of a single statutory section, § 56.181 — they are not independent of one another. This clause states the revocation, sample-destruction, security, and access/deletion mechanisms the statute's own text requires; it does not state what "reasonable security procedures and practices" specifically requires beyond that general statutory language, and it does not address the separate consent-menu requirement of § 56.181(a)(2) or the nondiscrimination and insurer/employer disclosure restrictions of § 56.181(e)-(f), each covered in a companion clause.

NONDISCRIMINATION FOR EXERCISING RIGHTS, AND RESTRICTION ON DISCLOSURE TO INSURERS AND EMPLOYERS
The statute also restricts what a company may do in response to a consumer's exercise of rights, and to whom it may disclose genetic data. Civil Code § 56.181(e) provides that a person or public entity shall not discriminate against a consumer because the consumer exercised rights under the statute, including by denying goods, services, or benefits, charging different prices or rates (including through discounts, incentives, or penalties), providing a different level or quality of goods, services, or benefits, suggesting the consumer would receive different treatment, or treating the exercise of rights as a basis for suspicion of criminal wrongdoing. Separately, § 56.181(f)(1) provides that, subject to a stated exception, a direct-to-consumer genetic testing company shall not disclose a consumer's genetic data to any entity responsible for administering or making decisions regarding health insurance, life insurance, long-term care insurance, disability insurance, or employment, or to any entity that provides advice to such an entity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A person or public entity shall not discriminate against a consumer because the consumer exercised any of the consumer’s rights under this chapter by doing any of the following, including, but not limited to: (1) Denying goods, services, or benefits to the customer. (2) Charging different prices or rates for goods or services, including through the use of discounts or other incentives or imposing penalties."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.181(e) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Genetic Information Privacy Act, nondiscrimination for exercising statutory rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.181.)
  "a direct-to-consumer genetic testing company shall not disclose a consumer’s genetic data to any entity that is responsible for administering or making decisions regarding health insurance, life insurance, long-term care insurance, disability insurance, or employment or to any entity that provides advice to an entity that is responsible for performing those functions."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.181(f)(1) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Genetic Information Privacy Act, restriction on disclosure to insurance and employment decisionmakers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.181.)
  Known gap: Both citations are subsections of a single statutory section, § 56.181 — they are not independent of one another. This clause states the statute's nondiscrimination rule and its restriction on disclosure to insurance- and employment-decision entities; it does not restate the statute's own exception to that disclosure restriction, set out in § 56.181(f)(2), for an entity not primarily engaged in those functions whose relevant agents or divisions are walled off from the data, and it does not address the separate consent, revocation, security, or notice obligations covered in companion clauses.

ENFORCEMENT: CIVIL PENALTIES PROSECUTED BY PUBLIC OFFICIALS
The statute states its own civil penalty amounts and names who may bring an enforcement action. Civil Code § 56.182(a) provides that a person who negligently violates the statute shall be assessed a civil penalty of up to one thousand dollars ($1,000) plus court costs. Section 56.182(b) provides that a person who willfully violates the statute shall be assessed a civil penalty of not less than one thousand dollars ($1,000) and not more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) plus court costs. Under § 56.182(c), actions for relief under the statute must be prosecuted exclusively in a court of competent jurisdiction by the Attorney General, a district attorney, an authorized county counsel, or specified city attorneys or city prosecutors, in the name of the People of the State of California, brought upon their own complaint, upon the complaint of a board, officer, person, corporation, or association, or upon the complaint of a person who has suffered injury in fact and lost money or property as a result of the violation. Section 56.182(d) provides that penalties recovered under the statute are paid to the individual to whom the genetic data at issue pertains.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any person who negligently violates this chapter shall be assessed a civil penalty in an amount not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) plus court costs, as determined by the court."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.182(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Genetic Information Privacy Act, civil penalty amount for negligent violations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.182.)
  "Any person who willfully violates this chapter shall be assessed a civil penalty in an amount not less than one thousand dollars ($1,000) and not more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) plus court costs, as determined by the court."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.182(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Genetic Information Privacy Act, civil penalty amount for willful violations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.182.)
  "Actions for relief pursuant to this chapter shall be prosecuted exclusively in a court of competent jurisdiction by the Attorney General or a district attorney or by a county counsel authorized by agreement with the district attorney in actions involving violation of a county ordinance, or by a city attorney of a city having a population in excess of 750,000, or by a city attorney in a city and county or, with the consent of the district attorney, by a city prosecutor in a city having a full-time city prosecutor in the name of the people of the State of California upon their own complaint or upon the complaint of a board, officer, person, corporation, or association, or upon a complaint by a person who has suffered injury in fact and has lost money or property as a result of the violation of this chapter."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.182(c) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Genetic Information Privacy Act, exclusive prosecution by public officials (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.182.)
  "Penalties recovered pursuant to this section shall be paid to the individual to whom the genetic data at issue pertains."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.182(d) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Genetic Information Privacy Act, disposition of recovered penalties (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.182.)
  Known gap: All four citations are subsections of a single statutory section, § 56.182 — they are not independent of one another. The statute's own text places prosecution of a violation exclusively in the hands of the named public officials; on this text, it does not give a consumer a standalone civil claim to file and litigate directly the way some other California privacy statutes do — a consumer's own complaint of injury in fact is instead one stated basis on which a public official may choose to bring an action, and a consumer to whom the genetic data pertains is the one to whom any penalty ultimately recovered is paid. Whether some other statute (for example, the state's Unfair Competition Law) supplies a separate, independent avenue was not researched for this clause and is not addressed here.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate that Jordan T. Reyes, on behalf of Acme, Inc., has received and reviewed this information sheet describing California's Genetic Information Privacy Act.

Prepared by: Jordan T. Reyes
On behalf of: Acme, Inc.
Date: September 1, 2026

Separately, § 56.181(f)(1) provides that, subject to a stated exception, a direct-to-consumer genetic testing company shall not disclose a consumer's genetic data to any entity responsible for administering or making decisions regarding health insurance, life insurance, long-term care insurance, disability insurance, or employment, or to any entity that provides advice to such an entity.

citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, nondiscrimination for exercising statutory rights
citations.quote: A person or public entity shall not discriminate against a consumer because the consumer exercised any of the consumer’s rights under this chapter by doing any of the following, including, but not limited to: (1) Denying goods, services, or benefits to the customer. (2) Charging different prices or rates for goods or services, including through the use of discounts or other incentives or imposing penalties.

citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, restriction on disclosure to insurance and employment decisionmakers
citations.quote: a direct-to-consumer genetic testing company shall not disclose a consumer’s genetic data to any entity that is responsible for administering or making decisions regarding health insurance, life insurance, long-term care insurance, disability insurance, or employment or to any entity that provides advice to an entity that is responsible for performing those functions.

expectedJSON.gap: Both citations are subsections of a single statutory section, § 56.181 — they are not independent of one another. This clause states the statute's nondiscrimination rule and its restriction on disclosure to insurance- and employment-decision entities; it does not restate the statute's own exception to that disclosure restriction, set out in § 56.181(f)(2), for an entity not primarily engaged in those functions whose relevant agents or divisions are walled off from the data, and it does not address the separate consent, revocation, security, or notice obligations covered in companion clauses.

expectedJSON.body: The statute states its own civil penalty amounts and names who may bring an enforcement action. Civil Code § 56.182(a) provides that a person who negligently violates the statute shall be assessed a civil penalty of up to one thousand dollars ($1,000) plus court costs. Section 56.182(b) provides that a person who willfully violates the statute shall be assessed a civil penalty of not less than one thousand dollars ($1,000) and not more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) plus court costs. Under § 56.182(c), actions for relief under the statute must be prosecuted exclusively in a court of competent jurisdiction by the Attorney General, a district attorney, an authorized county counsel, or specified city attorneys or city prosecutors, in the name of the People of the State of California, brought upon their own complaint, upon the complaint of a board, officer, person, corporation, or association, or upon the complaint of a person who has suffered injury in fact and lost money or property as a result of the violation. Section 56.182(d) provides that penalties recovered under the statute are paid to the individual to whom the genetic data at issue pertains.

citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, civil penalty amount for negligent violations
citations.quote: Any person who negligently violates this chapter shall be assessed a civil penalty in an amount not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) plus court costs, as determined by the court.

citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, civil penalty amount for willful violations
citations.quote: Any person who willfully violates this chapter shall be assessed a civil penalty in an amount not less than one thousand dollars ($1,000) and not more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) plus court costs, as determined by the court.

citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, exclusive prosecution by public officials
citations.quote: Actions for relief pursuant to this chapter shall be prosecuted exclusively in a court of competent jurisdiction by the Attorney General or a district attorney or by a county counsel authorized by agreement with the district attorney in actions involving violation of a county ordinance, or by a city attorney of a city having a population in excess of 750,000, or by a city attorney in a city and county or, with the consent of the district attorney, by a city prosecutor in a city having a full-time city prosecutor in the name of the people of the State of California upon their own complaint or upon the complaint of a board, officer, person, corporation, or association, or upon a complaint by a person who has suffered injury in fact and has lost money or property as a result of the violation of this chapter.

citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, disposition of recovered penalties
citations.quote: Penalties recovered pursuant to this section shall be paid to the individual to whom the genetic data at issue pertains.

expectedJSON.gap: All four citations are subsections of a single statutory section, § 56.182 — they are not independent of one another. The statute's own text places prosecution of a violation exclusively in the hands of the named public officials; on this text, it does not give a consumer a standalone civil claim to file and litigate directly the way some other California privacy statutes do — a consumer's own complaint of injury in fact is instead one stated basis on which a public official may choose to bring an action, and a consumer to whom the genetic data pertains is the one to whom any penalty ultimately recovered is paid. Whether some other statute (for example, the state's Unfair Competition Law) supplies a separate, independent avenue was not researched for this clause and is not addressed here.
